theme: The kinsman-redeemer; redemption; the Davidic lineage
readingInstruction: Read Ruth 3:1-4:22. The story reaches its climax at the threshing floor and the city gate. Watch how Boaz acts as a redeemer, and how the chapter ends with a genealogy. That list of names is the point of the whole book.
settingTheScene: The barley harvest is ending, and Naomi is thinking about Ruth’s future. She devises a plan that is culturally daring: Ruth should go to the threshing floor at night and ask Boaz to act as the kinsman-redeemer. Boaz, who has already shown his generosity, is willing, but there is a closer relative who has the first right. Boaz goes to the city gate, the place of legal business, and settles the matter before ten elders. The story ends with a marriage, the birth of a son, and a genealogy that reaches to King David. For readers of Judges, this is a stunning turn: from “no king in Israel” to the line of the king.
observation: Naomi says, “My daughter, should I not seek rest for you, that it may be well with you?” (3:1).
Ruth lies at Boaz’s feet at night, and asks him to “spread your wings over your servant, for you are a redeemer” (3:9).
Boaz blesses her: “You have made your last kindness greater than the first” and calls her “a worthy woman” (3:10-11).
He tells her that there is a redeemer nearer than he, and promises to settle the matter that day (3:12-13).
At the gate, Boaz tells the nearer redeemer about the land of Elimelech, and the man says he will redeem it. When Boaz adds that he must also take Ruth, the man declines (4:1-6).
Boaz declares before the elders that he will redeem the property and marry Ruth “to perpetuate the name of the dead in his inheritance” (4:9-10).
The women say to Naomi, “Blessed be the LORD, who has not left you this day without a redeemer” (4:14).
The child Obed is born, and the book ends with a genealogy: Obed fathered Jesse, and Jesse fathered David (4:17-22).
interpretation:
The scene at the threshing floor can be misunderstood by modern readers. Ruth’s request, to “spread your wings over your servant,” is a request for marriage and protection. The same word for “wings” was used by Boaz in chapter 2, when he prayed that Ruth would find refuge under the wings of the LORD. Now Ruth asks Boaz to be that refuge, and he is the answer to his own prayer. The scene is full of integrity. Boaz does not take advantage of the situation. He sends Ruth away before dawn to protect her reputation, and he deals with the legal question openly.

The core of the story is redemption. Under the law of Moses, a close relative could “redeem” a family member who had fallen into poverty by buying back land or marrying a widow to raise children in the dead man’s name. The redeemer needed three things: he had to be a relative, he had to be able to pay, and he had to be willing. The nearer redeemer was a relative and was apparently able, but he was not willing when he learned the cost. Boaz is all three. He stands at the gate and takes on the burden of the family at personal cost.

Boaz’s actions are a picture of Christ. He is a relative, close to those he redeems. He is able to pay the price. He is willing, even when it costs him. Jesus became our brother in flesh and blood (Hebrews 2:14-17) so that he could redeem us. He paid the price with his own blood (1 Peter 1:18-19), and he did so willingly. “For the joy that was set before him he endured the cross” (Hebrews 12:2). The story invites us to see ourselves in Ruth, a stranger who was brought in and given a name and a place.

The ending is a surprise. The women of Bethlehem celebrate with Naomi, and she who was empty is now full. The baby Obed is placed in her arms. And then the genealogy reveals the reason the story was preserved: Obed is the grandfather of David. The Moabite Ruth is the great-grandmother of Israel’s greatest king. And Matthew’s Gospel will continue the list: David is the ancestor of Jesus Christ. The story that began in famine and death ends with the line of the Messiah.

The book of Judges ended with the cry for a king. Ruth does not answer it directly, but it provides the beginning of the answer. God is working, in obscure fields and city gates, through obedient and ordinary people, to bring about the king. Even in the days of the judges, God was preparing the way.
connection: The kinsman-redeemer laws are in Leviticus 25:25-55 and Deuteronomy 25:5-10. The theme of redemption appears in Job 19:25, Isaiah 41-54, and Galatians 4:4-5. Ruth, a Moabite, is named in Matthew 1:5, and Rahab too. The genealogy of Perez, Judah’s son, recalls Genesis 38 and 49:8-12. David’s line leads to Christ in Luke 1:32 and Romans 1:3.
application:
First, receive Boaz as a picture of Christ. He is near, able, and willing. Consider what that means for the debts you cannot pay: guilt, shame, and failure. Say aloud, “I have a Redeemer.”

Second, reflect on Boaz’s integrity. In a situation where he could have taken advantage, he acted honorably and openly. Where do you face a similar temptation? Choose to act with integrity this week.

Third, take heart from the genealogy. God’s work is often hidden in ordinary lives. The faithfulness of one widow, one landowner, and one baby changed history. Ask the Lord to use your small acts of obedience for purposes you may never see.
prayerPrompts: Thank Jesus for being a redeemer who is near, able, and willing.
Thank God for bringing a stranger into the line of the king, as he brought you in.
Ask him to make you faithful in ordinary things.
